title: Structs versus classes (value vs reference types)
hook: Structs are value types — assignment copies the data. Classes are reference types — assignment copies a pointer to the same object. Pick the right one and you avoid subtle bugs and performance traps.

blocks.text: A **struct** is a **value type**: the variable holds the data directly. Assigning or passing a struct copies all its fields. A **class** is a **reference type**: the variable holds a reference to a heap object. Many variables can point at the same class instance. Microsoft recommends structs for small data with value semantics — coordinates, colors, cache keys — not for your worker host.

entries.plainDefinition: A value type defined with the `struct` keyword. Assignment copies the fields.
entries.example: `readonly struct Point(int x, int y)` — copied on assignment.

entries.plainDefinition: A struct where instance members cannot mutate state. Enables zero-copy `in` parameters.
entries.example: `readonly struct CacheKey` — safe to pass with `in`.

entries.plainDefinition: Wrapping a value type inside a reference-type object on the heap. Happens when casting a struct to `object` or an interface.
entries.example: `object boxed = 42;` — the `int` is copied to the heap.

entries.plainDefinition: A struct with built-in value equality and `with`-expressions (module 05). Still a value type.

blocks.text: Choosing struct versus class affects correctness, performance, and API design. A mutable struct in a property getter mutates a copy and drops the write — a classic bug. A large struct copied through many method layers wastes CPU. A readonly struct with `in` parameters avoids both problems on hot paths like cache-key lookups.

blocks.title: Structs cannot inherit from classes
blocks.body: Structs can implement interfaces but cannot inherit from another class or struct. They implicitly inherit from `System.ValueType`. Use a class when you need inheritance or shared identity.

items.title: Struct assignment
items.body: Copies all fields. The two variables are independent. Mutating one does not affect the other.

items.title: Class assignment
items.body: Copies the reference. Both variables point at the same heap object. Mutations are shared.

items.title: Struct in a method parameter
items.body: Ordinary passing copies the struct. Use `ref` or `in` to alias instead (previous topic).

items.title: Struct in an array
items.body: Elements are stored inline. Mutating `array[i].Field` changes the array element directly.

diagram.title: Struct copy vs class alias
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  subgraph structCopy [Struct assignment]
    S1[a.X=1] --> S2[b=a copies fields]
    S2 --> S3[b.X=2 does not change a]
  end
  subgraph classAlias [Class assignment]
    C1[a.Total=1] --> C2[b=a copies ref]
    C2 --> C3[b.Total=2 changes a too]
  end

snippet.label: readonly struct key versus class client
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `RedisKey` is a small copied value — no identity. Line 8: `RedisGateway` is a class because it represents a connection-shaped collaborator with behavior and lifetime.

snippet.label: The mutable struct property trap
snippet.explanation: Line 8: `c.Box.Value = 99` calls the getter (copy), mutates the copy, and discards it. The original `Box` in `Container` is unchanged. This is why mutable structs in properties are dangerous.

snippet.label: Boxing a struct
snippet.code:
int count = 42;
object boxed = count;        // boxing — heap allocation
IComparable comp = count;    // boxing via interface

var list = new ArrayList { 1, 2, 3 }; // every int boxes
snippet.explanation: Line 2: assigning an `int` to `object` wraps it on the heap. Line 3: interface dispatch on a value type also boxes. Line 5: non-generic collections box every element — a performance trap in hot loops.

blocks.title: Value types in C# vs JS/TS
rows: `struct` — real copy semantics in the CLR
No equivalent — even `Date` is an object
TS `type Point = { x: number }` is still a JS object at runtime
Struct copies fields; class copies reference
Object equality is reference identity unless you compare fields manually

blocks.title: Mutable structs in properties
blocks.body: `container.Box.Value = 99` mutates a copy from the getter, not the stored struct. Keep structs immutable or mutate through a method on the containing class.

blocks.title: Large structs on hot paths
blocks.body: A 64-byte struct passed through ten method layers means ten copies. Use `readonly struct` with `in`, or switch to a class if the data is large or has identity.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: Microsoft design guidelines say prefer class unless the type is small (often cited as under 16 bytes), immutable, and short-lived — but measure copy cost on your hot path, not folklore. readonly struct plus in parameters avoids defensive copies in SkiaSharp-style math pipelines. Mutable struct in List<T> indexer is the classic interview trap — container.Box.Value = 1 mutates a copy from the getter. For Redis cache keys, readonly record struct beats class when equality is value-based and allocation must stay low.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying struct is always on the stack. Mutable struct in a collection without explaining copy semantics. Picking struct for a 200-byte DTO because 'structs are faster'. Not mentioning readonly struct with in.

interviewTakeaways: Struct copies on assignment; class aliases.
readonly struct pairs with in to avoid defensive copies.
Mutable struct property set mutates a copy from the getter.
60s: Small immutable data as readonly struct. Identity and dispose as class. List indexer copy trap. Measure, do not guess size cutoff.
Follow-up: when does boxing a struct negate the benefit?
commonPitfalls: Mutable structs in properties — set never persists.
Large structs copied through layers without in/readonly.
Strong answer: 'readonly struct for small immutable values. class for identity and dispose. Know list indexer and property getter copy traps.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript has primitives and objects. There is no custom value type; even `Date` is an object. C# lets you declare copy semantics with `struct`.
TypeScript `type Point = { x: number; y: number }` is still a JavaScript object at runtime. C# `struct Point` is a real value type in the CLR.
